The Crested satinbird (Cnemophilus macgregorii), a poorly known passerine endemic to the montane forests of New Guinea, produces a single, unusually large egg. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg is estimated at 13.55 grams [Ww0 = 13.55 grams], a value derived from standard measurements of egg length at 38.9 millimeters and width at 25.8 millimeters, which yield a volume consistent with this mass. This substantial egg represents a considerable maternal investment, rivaling the relative egg sizes of some megapodes. Under the thermal conditions typical of the nest microclimate at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the developing embryo requires approximately 26 days [ab = approximately 26 days] to complete development, although this estimate for the age at birth remains tentative and may be refined by future nest observations conducted at a slightly different incubation temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. The prolonged incubation period aligns with the species' slow life-history pace among the Paradisaeidae, although data from congeneric species remain sparse.

Under the active metabolic body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], fledging occurs at 25 days after hatching [tx = 25 days after hatching], marking the end of a brief but intensive nestling period. During this interval, the chick is entirely dependent on parental provisioning. Females attain a maximum adult wet weight of approximately 97.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 97.5 grams], while males, which are the larger sex in this dimorphic species, reach an average ultimate wet weight of around 105 grams [Wwi = around 105 grams]. This sexual size dimorphism is typical of polygynous birds-of-paradise and is thought to result from sexual selection on male body size. The substantial increase from the modest hatchling mass to these adult values underscores the efficiency of parental care during the nestling and early fledgling stages.

Sexual maturation is a protracted process in this species, with puberty estimated to occur at 75 days after hatching [tp = 75 days after hatching] at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively late age at reproductive maturity, in comparison to many smaller-bodied passerines, likely reflects the time required to complete skeletal growth and attain the adult body mass necessary to support reproductive effort. However, actual first reproduction in the wild is thought to be deferred considerably beyond the point of initial gonadal maturity. Based on extrapolations from the closely related congener Cnemophilus loriae, the age at first successful brood is estimated at 1.8 years [tR = 1.8 years] (or approximately 657 days) after hatching under the thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a delay that may be linked to the challenges of establishing a territory in a competitive lekking system.

The species exhibits an exceptionally low maximum reproductive rate, with females typically producing a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and field data indicate they likely raise only one such clutch per year [F_R_i = one such clutch per year]. This extremely slow annual reproductive output is among the lowest recorded for any passerine and is presumably a consequence of the high energetic cost of producing a very large egg, coupled with a long period of dependency during which the nestling is provisioned. The measured resting metabolic rate of adult birds at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] is 134 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 134 milliliters of oxygen per hour], providing an estimate of the basal maintenance costs that constrain how much energy can be diverted toward reproduction.

Maximum lifespan in the Crested satinbird appears to be considerable, with estimates based on the related species Cnemophilus loriae suggesting that individuals may live for 13.4 years [am = 13.4 years] at an active body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This longevity estimate, while derived from a congener, aligns with the general pattern observed in many birds-of-paradise, where slow life histories and low annual reproductive output are offset by high adult survival and extended reproductive lifespans. The slow pace of development reflects the constraints imposed by the stable but resource-limited montane environment of New Guinea, where a large egg investment early in life is balanced by prolonged adult survival. Future field studies measuring metabolic rates and documenting precise incubation temperatures will refine these preliminary life-history parameters.
